v: Soon afterwards, he went about through cities and villages, preaching and bringing the good news of God’s Kingdom. With him were the twelve,
and certain women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
and Joanna, the wife of Chuzas, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others; who served them from their possessions.
b: This passage tells us that Jesus traveled through towns and villages proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God, and it names several important women who followed him. They had been set free and rescued through his healing. These women followed Jesus not only in spirit; they also supported his ministry with their own resources, showing their gratitude and love for him.

Here we see the universal reach of the gospel. Not only the male disciples but women, too, played an important part in Jesus' ministry. Their names and backgrounds show that Jesus' salvation knows no distinction of gender or class. Whether a woman like Mary, who had been tormented by demons, or a woman like Joanna, who came from Herod's household, each was welcomed and used by Jesus.

This passage also reminds us that on the road of following Jesus, we do more than listen and pray. We can support God's work through practical action. Whether by giving financially or serving in other ways, it is an expression of our love for the Lord.
q: How do you practically support God's work in your daily life? Is there a new way you could serve the Lord better and show your love?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us the example of the women who faithfully followed Jesus. Help us, on the road of following him, to serve you not only with our hearts but also with our actions. May we, like these women, become supporters of your work in your kingdom, to the glory of your name. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When a great multitude came together, and people from every city were coming to him, he spoke by a parable.
“The farmer went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the road, and it was trampled under foot, and the birds of the sky devoured it.
Other seed fell on the rock, and as soon as it grew, it withered away, because it had no moisture.
Other fell amid the thorns, and the thorns grew with it, and choked it.
Other fell into the good ground, and grew, and produced one hundred times as much fruit.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!”
b: This passage is Jesus' famous parable of the sower, which describes how different kinds of soil affect the growth of the seed. The soils represent different conditions of the human heart, and the seed represents the word of God. Through this parable, Jesus teaches people how to receive and respond to God's word.

The soil along the path represents those whose hearts are closed, so that God's word has no effect on them. The rocky soil represents those who receive it briefly but have no root, and who cannot stand firm when trouble comes. The thorny ground represents those who are choked by the worries and temptations of the world, so that God's word cannot bear fruit in them. Only the good soil represents those who open their hearts and are willing to receive God's word, and they bear abundant fruit.

Jesus stresses, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," reminding us to listen to God's word with our whole heart and to examine the state of our spiritual life. Is our heart that good soil, able to bear a hundredfold?
q: Are you willing to let your heart become that good soil, receiving God's word and bearing fruit? How can you cultivate and maintain this spiritual condition in your life every day?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for the teaching of Jesus that helps us become good soil, able to bear a hundredfold. Make our hearts soft and open to receive your word, and help us live it out, to the glory of your name. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Then his disciples asked him, “What does this parable mean?”
He said, “To you it is given to know the mysteries of God’s Kingdom, but to the rest in parables; that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.
Those along the road are those who hear, then the devil comes, and takes away the word from their heart, that they may not believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are they who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; but these have no root, who believe for a while, then fall away in time of temptation.
That which fell among the thorns, these are those who have heard, and as they go on their way they are choked with cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and bring no fruit to maturity.
Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.
b: In this passage, Jesus explains to his disciples the parable of the sower he had told earlier, helping them understand the mysteries of the kingdom of God more deeply. Jesus points out that the seed represents the word of God, and the different soils represent different conditions of the heart. He emphasizes the response to hearing the word and its outcome, so that the disciples would understand that different attitudes of heart lead to different spiritual results.

Jesus describes four kinds of hearts. The first is "the path," representing those who hear the word but do not hold on to it; the devil quickly takes the word from their hearts so that they cannot be saved. The second is "the rock," those who receive the word with joy at first, but because they have no root, they lose faith as soon as trouble comes. The third is "the thorns," those who receive the word but are so absorbed in worldly things that the word finally cannot bear fruit in them. Only the fourth, "the good soil," represents those with an honest and good heart who hold fast to God's word, and they bear abundant fruit in their spiritual lives.

This passage invites us to examine the condition of our hearts. Have we truly let God's word take root in us and patiently bear fruit? Or is our faith troubled by the worries, riches, or pleasures of the world, so that we cannot bear fruit? Jesus hopes our hearts will be like "good soil," patiently holding on to the word and bearing a hundredfold.
q: In your spiritual life, are you rooted in the "good soil"? How do you keep your heart pure so that God's word bears abundant fruit in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us the wisdom to understand the parable of the sower. Make our hearts good soil that holds fast to your word and bears abundant fruit in our lives. Help us turn away from the temptations of the world, focus on your word, and persevere to the end, until we see your glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “No one, when he has lit a lamp, covers it with a container, or puts it under a bed; but puts it on a stand, that those who enter in may see the light.
For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed; nor anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.”
b: In this passage, Jesus uses the picture of a lamp and light to teach his disciples how to live out God's word. He stresses that since we have received God's truth, we should be like a lamp, letting its light shine before others rather than hiding it. Jesus reminds his disciples that whatever we hide, whether our actions or our thoughts, will in the end be revealed before God, for God knows all things.

In this passage the "lamp" represents the word and truth of God that we have received, and the "lampstand" represents the witness of our lives. When we live out God's word and let his light show in our actions and words, that light will draw others, so that they too can see and be moved by God's truth. At the same time, Jesus reminds us to be careful how we listen, because truth that we hear and receive but do not apply in our lives loses its power. He warns that those who have but do not use well may in the end lose even what they have.

This passage reminds us that we must not only receive God's word but put it into practice, so that our lives become a shining example for others. We should watch whether we are showing God's truth in our daily lives, and make sure that the truth we hear guides our actions. Only then can we truly become shining witnesses in God's kingdom.
q: How can you be a shining example to others in your daily life? Are you putting God's word into practice and living out God's truth before others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us your word. Help us to be not merely hearers but doers of the word. Let our lives be like a lamp that lights up this dark world and draws more people to you. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: His mother and brothers came to him, and they could not come near him for the crowd.
Some people told him, “Your mother and your brothers stand outside, desiring to see you.”
But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are these who hear the word of God, and do it.”
b: In this passage, Jesus expresses through his words an important spiritual truth: true spiritual relationships go beyond blood relationships. When Jesus' mother and brothers came to find him, he used the occasion to teach the crowd that those who hear God's word and do it are the ones who truly have a spiritual relationship with him.

Jesus' reply is not meant to belittle family ties but to stress the importance of the spiritual family. It shows that our relationship with God is based not on outward status or position but on hearing and doing his word. Those who hear God's word and obey it are truly members of God's household. Whatever our background, it is only by obeying and doing God's word that we become Jesus' family.

This passage reminds us that relationships in the spiritual life matter far more than blood ties. We need to ask ourselves whether we truly listen to and obey God's word, and so become the "mother" and "brothers" whom Jesus commends. Only through obedience to God's word can we truly find our place in the spiritual family and have a deep union with Christ.
q: How do you practically obey God's word in your life? Have you found your place in the spiritual family and built a deep relationship with Christ?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for bringing us into your spiritual family. Help us not only to hear your word but to live it out, and to become the people who please you. May our lives be closely joined to Christ, and may we find our belonging in his household. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now on one of those days, he entered into a boat, himself and his disciples, and he said to them, “Let’s go over to the other side of the lake.” So they launched out.
But as they sailed, he fell asleep. A wind storm came down on the lake, and they were taking on dangerous amounts of water.
They came to him, and awoke him, saying, “Master, master, we are dying!” He awoke, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water, and they ceased, and it was calm.
He said to them, “Where is your faith?” Being afraid they marveled, saying to one another, “Who is this then, that he commands even the winds and the water, and they obey him?”
b: In this passage we see a miracle that happened as Jesus and his disciples crossed the lake together. While the boat was sailing, a fierce storm suddenly arose, and the disciples were terrified, afraid the boat would sink. They hurried to wake Jesus, who was sleeping in the stern, and begged him to save them. When Jesus woke, he rebuked the wind and the waves, and at once they ceased and the lake became calm. This miracle shows Jesus' absolute authority over nature, and it also reveals the weakness of the disciples' faith.

Jesus then asked his disciples, "Where is your faith?" This question was not only about that moment; it also tested their trust in him. Although the disciples had already seen Jesus do many miracles, they still lacked faith when they faced danger. This passage reminds us that even in the storm Jesus is still with us and has the power to calm it, but can we hold on to our faith in him in times of danger?

Through this passage God teaches us that whatever storms we face in life, he is in control. We need to ask ourselves: in the storm, do we choose to trust Jesus, or do we fall into fear and anxiety? This passage encourages us to firmly believe, whatever our circumstances, in Jesus' presence and in his power to control all things.
q: How do you respond when you face the storms of life? In these hard times, how do you strengthen your trust in Jesus and seek his peace?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for being with us even in the storms of our lives. Strengthen our faith, so that in every difficulty we can rely on you, knowing that you are in control of everything. May we witness your peace and power in every storm. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: They arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is opposite Galilee.
When Jesus stepped ashore, a certain man out of the city who had demons for a long time met him. He wore no clothes, and didn’t live in a house, but in the tombs.
When he saw Jesus, he cried out, and fell down before him, and with a loud voice said, “What do I have to do with you, Jesus, you Son of the Most High God? I beg you, don’t torment me!”

For Jesus was commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. For the unclean spirit had often seized the man. He was kept under guard, and bound with chains and fetters. Breaking the bonds apart, he was driven by the demon into the desert.
Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered into him.
They begged him that he would not command them to go into the abyss.
Now there was there a herd of many pigs feeding on the mountain, and they begged him that he would allow them to enter into those. Then he allowed them.
The demons came out of the man, and entered into the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake, and were drowned.
b: This passage describes an amazing miracle Jesus performed in the region of the Gerasenes, where he drove many demons out of a man. This demon-possessed man lived in extreme suffering, far from society, wearing no clothes and living among the tombs, a picture of how completely lost he was under the demons' control. When he saw Jesus, the demons recognized Jesus' divinity, called him "Son of the Most High God," and begged him not to torment them.

Jesus drove out the demons with absolute authority and allowed them to enter a herd of pigs nearby. The herd then rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned, showing that even the evil power of demons cannot stand against Jesus' authority. This miracle shows Jesus' victory over all evil spirits, and it also shows that he came to set free those held captive by the powers of darkness.

This passage reminds us that Jesus has complete authority and can set us free from every spiritual bondage and oppression. Whatever difficulty or inner struggle we face, we should seek Jesus' deliverance, because he can bring complete freedom and renewal. We should trust his power and entrust our fears and struggles to him, for he is our only Savior.
q: What bondage or struggles in your life need Jesus' deliverance? How do you seek and trust Jesus' power to find freedom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us Jesus Christ, our Deliverer and Savior. Help us rely on Jesus' power to be free from all bondage and oppression, and let us find complete freedom in his peace. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When those who fed them saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country.
People went out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.
Those who saw it told them how he who had been possessed by demons was healed.
All the people of the surrounding country of the Gadarenes asked him to depart from them, for they were very much afraid. Then he entered into the boat and returned.
But the man from whom the demons had gone out begged him that he might go with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying,
“Return to your house, and declare what great things God has done for you.” He went his way, proclaiming throughout the whole city what great things Jesus had done for him.
b: In this passage we see the reaction to the miracle Jesus performed in the region of the Gerasenes. When the local people heard about the tragedy of the pigs and that the demon-possessed man had been set free, they came out to see. They saw the man who had once been raving now sitting at Jesus' feet, clothed and in his right mind, and the sight filled them with fear. Although they witnessed the miracle, they were afraid of Jesus' power and begged him to leave.

The man who had been demon-possessed reacted very differently. He begged to be with Jesus, because he had experienced Jesus' salvation and grace. But Jesus sent him home and told him to tell everyone what God had done for him. This command shows that Jesus' mission is not only to save individuals but also to spread God's love and salvation through the testimony of those individuals.

This passage reminds us that everyone saved by God has a responsibility to bear witness to this grace, so that more people may know what God has done. Though some may reject Jesus out of fear or misunderstanding, we still need to faithfully proclaim what he has done, because this is precisely our mission after receiving grace and salvation.
q: Do you have opportunities in your life to testify to the great things God has done for you? How can you share your testimony more boldly and pass God's love on to others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for letting us experience your redemption and grace. Give us courage to faithfully bear witness to what you have done and to proclaim your love and salvation. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When Jesus returned, the multitude welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him.
Behold, a man named Jairus came. He was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell down at Jesus’ feet, and begged him to come into his house,
for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. But as he went, the multitudes pressed against him.
A woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her living on physicians and could not be healed by any
came behind him, and touched the fringe of his cloak. Immediately the flow of her blood stopped.
Jesus said, “Who touched me?” When all denied it, Peter and those with him said, “Master, the multitudes press and jostle you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”
But Jesus said, “Someone did touch me, for I perceived that power has gone out of me.”

When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared to him in the presence of all the people the reason why she had touched him, and how she was healed immediately.
He said to her, “Daughter, cheer up. Your faith has made you well. Go in peace.”
While he still spoke, one from the ruler of the synagogue’s house came, saying to him, “Your daughter is dead. Don’t trouble the Teacher.”
But Jesus hearing it, answered him, “Don’t be afraid. Only believe, and she will be healed.”
When he came to the house, he didn’t allow anyone to enter in, except Peter, John, James, the father of the child, and her mother.
All were weeping and mourning her, but he said, “Don’t weep. She isn’t dead, but sleeping.”
They were ridiculing him, knowing that she was dead.
But he put them all outside, and taking her by the hand, he called, saying, “Child, arise!”
Her spirit returned, and she rose up immediately. He commanded that something be given to her to eat.
Her parents were amazed, but he commanded them to tell no one what had been done.
b: This passage records two interwoven miracles: the raising of Jairus' daughter and the healing of the woman with the issue of blood. They are not only a display of Jesus' power but a deep revelation about faith and hope.

When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, a scene full of longing and expectation. Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue and a man of standing in society, fell at Jesus' feet for the sake of his beloved only daughter and begged him to come to his house and heal her. This was a father's love, and also faith in Jesus.

But on the way to Jairus' house, a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years quietly touched the fringe of Jesus' garment. Her illness made her unclean and unaccepted in both society and religion. Yet she believed in her heart, "If I just touch his garment, I will be made well." This faith touched the Lord. She was healed at once, and Jesus deliberately stopped, affirmed her action, and called her "daughter," a word of honor and acceptance.

Just as this healing ended, terrible news came: "Your daughter is dead." The words struck Jairus' heart like a cold spike. But Jesus said, "Don't be afraid. Only believe, and she will be healed." This sentence is the soul of the whole passage: believe even in despair, and there is hope even in the dark.

When Jesus came to Jairus' house, he took only three disciples and the child's parents into the grieving room. While everyone wept over the death, Jesus declared, "She is not dead, but sleeping." The people laughed at him, but with authority he called the girl's spirit back: "Child, arise!" The girl rose at once, showing Jesus' victory and authority over death.
This passage reminds us:
• No matter how long a problem has dragged on (like the twelve years of bleeding),
• No matter how hopeless the situation seems (like the death of Jairus' daughter),
• when faith is joined to Jesus, we will see his wonderful work.

Jesus does not only heal our bodies; he also restores our relationships, rebuilds our hope, and brings back what we thought was lost. He is willing to walk into our deepest darkness and bring life and light.
q: In the difficulties you face now, is there anything that makes you feel "it's too late" or "there's no hope left"? Today Jesus also says to you, "Don't be afraid. Only believe!" Are you willing to keep this word in your heart and live it out?
pr: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for never leaving or forsaking me in the storms and brokenness of my life. Increase my faith, so that even in situations that seem hopeless I can cling to you, believing that you have power to raise the dead and turn despair into joy. May I keep believing your word and holding on to your promises all my life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

v: He called the twelve together, and gave them power and authority over all demons, and to cure diseases.
He sent them out to preach God’s Kingdom and to heal the sick.
He said to them, “Take nothing for your journey—no staffs, nor wallet, nor bread, nor money. Don’t have two coats each.
Into whatever house you enter, stay there, and depart from there.
As many as don’t receive you, when you depart from that city, shake off even the dust from your feet for a testimony against them.”
They departed and went throughout the villages, preaching the Good News and healing everywhere.
b: In this passage, Jesus gives the twelve disciples authority and power and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and heal the sick. This is the first time the disciples, in the course of following Jesus, are formally commissioned for specific ministry. Jesus not only gave them power in the spirit; he also instructed them to depend on God's provision rather than worldly resources, so that they could wholeheartedly carry out the mission God had entrusted to them.

Jesus specially told the disciples not to take extra things, which emphasizes simplicity and complete trust in God. Jesus knew that when they relied entirely on God, they would experience his real provision and protection, and could focus on the work of the kingdom without being tied down by material things. He also taught them that if a place would not receive the gospel, they should shake the dust off their feet, a sign that they had faithfully delivered God's message and that those who rejected it would bear their own responsibility.

This passage reminds us that when God sends us out to serve, we must let go of dependence on material things and rely entirely on God's provision. Like the disciples, we should carry out God's mission with faith and obedience, knowing that all our needs are in his hands. Our ministry should not be bound by worldly possessions but should make God's kingdom the first goal.
q: In your service, do you depend on God's provision? How do you stay focused on God's mission even under material pressure?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us authority and power so that we can take part in your work. Help us let go of dependence on material things in our service, trust fully in your provision, and boldly proclaim your gospel. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all that was done by him; and he was very perplexed, because it was said by some that John had risen from the dead,
and by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the old prophets had risen again.
Herod said, “I beheaded John, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” He sought to see him.
b: This passage records Herod's confusion and anxiety after he heard about Jesus. Jesus' fame and the miracles he performed had spread everywhere, so that even Herod heard about them. Various rumors and guesses circulated among the people: some said Jesus was John risen from the dead, others thought he was Elijah or one of the ancient prophets appearing again. Because he had beheaded John, Herod was uneasy, and he wanted to know who this Jesus really was.

This passage shows that Jesus' fame and ministry had drawn wide attention in society at that time, and even the powerful were watching his movements. Herod's fear reflected the guilt in his heart and his curiosity about Jesus' identity. He could not understand Jesus' divinity, yet he was shaken by his work. It also shows that Jesus' coming and his ministry had a deep effect not only on ordinary people but even on the political powers of the day.

This passage reminds us that Jesus' influence reaches without limit. Whatever people think of him, his work challenges and overturns worldly power and ideas. As we think about Jesus' place in our lives, we too need, like Herod, to seek and come to know Jesus' true identity, and to reflect on how we respond to his call.
q: Who is Jesus to you? How do you respond to his call and challenge in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us your great power and love through Jesus Christ. Help us not only to hear about Jesus' deeds in our daily lives but to know him personally and respond to his call. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The apostles, when they had returned, told him what things they had done. He took them and withdrew apart to a desert region of a city called Bethsaida.
But the multitudes, perceiving it, followed him. He welcomed them, spoke to them of God’s Kingdom, and he cured those who needed healing.

The day began to wear away; and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the multitude away, that they may go into the surrounding villages and farms, and lodge, and get food, for we are here in a deserted place.”
But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish, unless we should go and buy food for all these people.”
For they were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples, “Make them sit down in groups of about fifty each.”
They did so, and made them all sit down.
He took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to the sky, he blessed them, broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the multitude.
They ate and were all filled. They gathered up twelve baskets of broken pieces that were left over.
b: This passage records Jesus' miracle of the five loaves and two fish, in which he fed five thousand people. This miracle strongly shows Jesus' divinity and his compassion for the crowd. When the disciples felt helpless before the people's need, Jesus met that need with his limitless power. He was not at a loss because supplies were limited; in faith he entrusted the five loaves and two fish to God and performed this astonishing miracle.

Jesus taught his disciples to face the challenge before them with faith and to believe that God's provision is limitless. The disciples had thought it impossible to meet the needs of so many people, but Jesus' action let them see God's abundance and his supernatural power. This miracle not only met a material need; it was also a spiritual lesson, reminding the disciples to rely on God in their service rather than on their own strength.

This passage reminds us that however great the challenge we face, we should depend on God's provision with faith. Jesus shows that when we offer what little we have, God will wonderfully use and bless it, accomplishing more than we can imagine. This teaches us to learn to trust God's abundance and to witness his great power in every challenge.
q: When you face difficulties that seem unsolvable, how do you rely on God's provision? Are you willing to entrust the little you have to God and let him accomplish something greater?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing your abundant provision through Jesus. Strengthen our faith, so that in challenges and difficulties we rely on your power and witness your miracles and wonders. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As he was praying alone, the disciples were with him, and he asked them, “Who do the multitudes say that I am?”
They answered, “ ‘John the Baptizer,’ but others say, ‘Elijah,’ and others, that one of the old prophets has risen again.”
He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered, “The Christ of God.”
But he warned them, and commanded them to tell this to no one,
saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things, and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and the third day be raised up.”
b: In this passage, Jesus first asks his disciples about his identity, leading them to think about the relationship between his work in the world and who he is. This is a vital question, because knowing Jesus' true identity is the heart of faith. When the disciples reported the crowd's various guesses about Jesus, Peter boldly declared that Jesus is "the Christ of God," showing his deep understanding of and faith in Jesus.

Jesus then told his disciples about the suffering and death he must face, and his resurrection on the third day. These words not only foretold Jesus' mission but also revealed the plan of redemption for which he came into the world. He made the disciples understand that, as the Christ, he must go through suffering, and this is the road that leads to salvation.

This passage reminds us that knowing Jesus' true identity is vital to our faith. Like Peter, can we boldly declare that Jesus is the Christ, and see God's plan of redemption in his suffering and resurrection? We are also called to accept this suffering Christ, to carry the cross with him, and to follow in his footsteps.
q: Do you clearly know that Jesus is the Christ, and do you declare who he is in your life? How do you walk with Jesus daily and receive the salvation he gives?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us your Son Jesus Christ, our Savior and the Christ. Strengthen our faith so that we may clearly know who Jesus is and boldly follow in his steps. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake, will save it.
For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, and loses or forfeits his own self?
For whoever will be ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed, when he comes in his glory, and the glory of the Father, and of the holy angels.
But I tell you the truth: There are some of those who stand here who will in no way taste of death until they see God’s Kingdom.”
b: In this passage, Jesus tells his disciples and those who follow him plainly the cost of being his disciple. He requires his followers to deny themselves and take up their cross daily. This means giving up a self-centered way of life and submitting completely to God's will. Jesus goes on to stress that whoever tries to save his own life will lose it, but whoever is willing to lose his life for Jesus' sake will find true life.

Jesus' teaching also reminds us that pursuing glory and success in the world is meaningless if it costs us our soul. Jesus warns that whoever is ashamed of him and his words will be rejected and put to shame when the kingdom of God comes. So he calls those who follow him to be faithful and unwavering, holding firmly to his teaching whatever challenge or pressure they face.

This passage calls us to reflect: are we truly willing to deny ourselves in order to follow Jesus? Are we willing to give up worldly gain and glory to pursue the values of God's kingdom? Jesus' call is for us to take up the cross in our daily lives, follow him steadfastly, and look forward to the full revealing of God's kingdom in our lives.
q: Are you willing to deny yourself in order to follow Jesus? How do you practically take up your cross and follow the Lord steadfastly in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for calling us to follow your Son Jesus Christ. Give us courage and strength to take up the cross in our daily lives and follow him faithfully. May we not be moved by the temptations of the world but walk steadfastly in his way. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: About eight days after these sayings, he took with him Peter, John, and James, and went up onto the mountain to pray.
As he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became white and dazzling.
Behold, two men were talking with him, who were Moses and Elijah,
who appeared in glory, and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they were fully awake, they saw his glory, and the two men who stood with him.
As they were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good for us to be here. Let’s make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah,” not knowing what he said.
While he said these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered into the cloud.
A voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!”
When the voice came, Jesus was found alone. They were silent, and told no one in those days any of the things which they had seen.
b: This passage records the scene on the mountain where Jesus' glory was revealed. Jesus took Peter, John, and James up the mountain to pray, and as he prayed his appearance was changed, showing the glory of his divinity. Moses and Elijah appeared on either side of Jesus, representing the witness of the Law and the Prophets, and they spoke with Jesus about the great work of redemption he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. The scene amazed Peter and the other disciples, and Peter even proposed building three shelters to commemorate the holy moment.

But while Peter was still speaking, a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud declaring that Jesus is God's Son, the Chosen One, and telling the disciples to listen to him. This voice not only confirmed Jesus' identity but also stressed his central place in God's plan of redemption. The experience filled the disciples with awe, yet they were told not to tell anyone for the time being.

This passage lets us see the revealing of Jesus' divinity. It reminds us that he is not merely a prophet or a teacher but the Son of God, who carries God's glory and the mission of redemption. Like those disciples, we should revere Jesus, listen to his teaching, and bear witness to his glory in our lives.
q: When you think about Jesus' divinity and glory, how does it affect your life of faith? How can you listen to his teaching better in your daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing your glory through Jesus Christ. Help us know more of Jesus' divinity and his important place in the plan of redemption. Let us listen to his teaching in our lives and bear witness to his glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great multitude met him.
Behold, a man from the crowd called out, saying, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
Behold, a spirit takes him, he suddenly cries out, and it convulses him so that he foams, and it hardly departs from him, bruising him severely.
I begged your disciples to cast it out, and they couldn’t.”
Jesus answered, “Faithless and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.”
While he was still coming, the demon threw him down and convulsed him violently. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
They were all astonished at the majesty of God. But while all were marveling at all the things which Jesus did, he said to his disciples,
b: This passage describes a father whom Jesus met after coming down from the mountain. His only son was possessed by a demon and suffered severe convulsions. The father had asked Jesus' disciples for help, but they could not drive the demon out. When Jesus heard this, he lamented the unbelief and perversity of that generation, and with his authority he rebuked the demon and the child was healed.

This passage reveals Jesus' sorrow over human unbelief, especially when his disciples could not overcome this challenge by faith, which shows all the more the importance of faith. Jesus stressed that faith is the key that drives miracles, while unbelief is the cause of failure. Here Jesus displays his limitless power and teaches the disciples the power of faith.

This passage reminds us that faith is the key to our connection with God and the foundation for witnessing his work. We need to examine whether our faith is enough and work to strengthen it in our lives, so that God's power can be shown in our difficulties. Like that father, we should seek Jesus' help in hardship and believe that his power can solve the problems we face.
q: When you face difficulties or challenges, do you rely on God with faith? How do you cultivate and strengthen your faith in daily life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing the power of faith through Jesus. Help us be more steadfast in faith, so that whatever difficulty we face, we rely completely on your power. May we witness your great power in hardship and face every challenge of life with faith. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: They were all astonished at the majesty of God. But while all were marveling at all the things which Jesus did, he said to his disciples,
“Let these words sink into your ears, for the Son of Man will be delivered up into the hands of men.”
But they didn’t understand this saying. It was concealed from them, that they should not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
b: In this passage, Jesus again tells his disciples of the suffering he is about to face. Although the disciples had seen the miracles Jesus did and his mighty power, they still found it hard to understand the meaning of what he foretold. Jesus told them to listen carefully to his words, especially his warning that he would be delivered up, which is part of his mission of redemption. Yet the true meaning of these words remained hidden from the disciples, and they neither understood it nor dared to ask him about it.

This passage shows that even the disciples closest to Jesus sometimes could not immediately understand God's plan and Jesus' mission. Jesus plainly foretold the suffering he would bear, yet his disciples were still shrouded in confusion. This reflects the limits of human understanding of God's plan, but it does not diminish the fulfillment of that plan. Jesus' words would finally be fulfilled in his suffering and resurrection, and after going through all of it the disciples would gradually understand.

This passage reminds us that when we meet confusion as our spiritual life grows, we should hold on in faith and humility and wait patiently for God's revelation. Even if for a time we cannot fully understand God's plan, we should still trust his word, and at the right time God will make his will clear to us.
q: When you meet confusion or things you don't understand in your faith, how do you respond? Can you trust God's plan and wait for the answer in his time?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us your word. Though at times we cannot fully understand it, give us faith to wait patiently for your revelation. Help us keep trusting you in our confusion and understand your will in the time you have set. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: An argument arose among them about which of them was the greatest.
Jesus, perceiving the reasoning of their hearts, took a little child, and set him by his side,
and said to them, “Whoever receives this little child in my name receives me. Whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For whoever is least among you all, this one will be great.”
b: This passage describes an argument among the disciples about which of them would be greatest in the kingdom of God. The argument shows they had not yet fully understood the humility and servanthood that Jesus taught. Jesus saw the thoughts of their hearts, and so he used a little child as an example to teach them about true greatness.

Jesus brought a little child to stand beside him and told the disciples that whoever welcomes such a child in his name welcomes Jesus himself, and so welcomes the Father who sent him. Jesus went on to teach that in God's kingdom, greatness lies not in position or power but in humility and service. Those who seem smallest and least noticeable in human eyes are the greatest in God's eyes.

This passage reminds us that in God's kingdom true greatness comes not from position or honor but from humility and a heart willing to serve others. When we learn to welcome and respect the little ones, especially those overlooked and marginalized in society, we are truly serving God. We should reflect on whether we put too much weight on status and neglect the humility and spirit of service that Jesus taught.
q: How do you put into practice the teaching of humility and serving others in your life? Are you willing, like Jesus, to welcome the little ones and respect them?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us that in your kingdom true greatness lies in humility and service. Help us let go of the pursuit of status, follow Jesus' example, and gladly welcome and serve others. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we forbade him, because he doesn’t follow with us.”
Jesus said to him, “Don’t forbid him, for he who is not against us is for us.”
b: In this passage, John reports to Jesus that he saw someone casting out demons in Jesus' name, but because that person did not follow along with the disciples, they tried to stop him. This shows the disciples' narrow view of how others serve Jesus: they thought only those who followed Jesus together with them were right. Jesus corrected their attitude and told them not to stop such a person, for whoever is not against them is for them.

Jesus' answer shows that his work and kingdom are broad, beyond what the disciples could grasp. He calls them to have a wide heart that welcomes different forms of service and following, as long as these people are truly working for God's kingdom. This passage reminds us that as Christians we should learn to be inclusive and to accept others' different ways of serving, rather than making our own understanding and methods absolute.

This passage encourages us to have a broader vision in our ministry and to see that God's kingdom is not limited to the ways and groups familiar to us. We should welcome and support those who, though their backgrounds and methods differ from ours, are also centered on Jesus and working for God's kingdom. This breadth of heart will help us work together better and extend God's kingdom.
q: In your ministry, are you able to accept and support Christians whose ways differ from yours? How do you keep a wide heart in extending God's kingdom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us to have a wide heart that accepts different forms of service. Help us see in our ministry that your kingdom is vast, and be willing to work with all who labor in your name to extend your kingdom together. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem
and sent messengers before his face. They went and entered into a village of the Samaritans, so as to prepare for him.
They didn’t receive him, because he was traveling with his face set toward Jerusalem.
When his disciples, James and John, saw this, they said, “Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from the sky, and destroy them, just as Elijah did?”
But he turned and rebuked them, “You don’t know of what kind of spirit you are.
For the Son of Man didn’t come to destroy men’s lives, but to save them.” They went to another village.
b: This passage records Jesus' determination to go to Jerusalem. On the way, in a Samaritan village, the people refused to welcome him because he was headed for Jerusalem. The disciples James and John suggested that Jesus call down fire from heaven to consume those who would not receive him, but Jesus rebuked them and reminded them that the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them.

This passage reveals Jesus' deep compassion for people. Even when rejected and opposed, he chose to respond with love and forgiveness rather than anger and punishment. Jesus' reaction stands in sharp contrast to the disciples' zeal and impulsiveness, and he made them understand that his mission is to bring salvation, not destruction. This teaching also shows that Jesus' kingdom is founded on grace and compassion, not on violence and revenge.

This passage reminds us that as Christians we should follow Jesus' compassion and forgiveness. Whatever rejection or hostility we face, we should choose to respond with love and grace. We should not be like the disciples, eager for punishment, but learn to keep compassion for others even in hard circumstances, which is exactly what Jesus teaches us.
q: How do you usually react when you face rejection or hostility? In those situations, can you, like Jesus, choose forgiveness and compassion?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for showing us, through Jesus Christ, an example of compassion and forgiveness. Help us, when we face rejection and hostility, to follow Jesus, respond to others with love and grace, and put his teaching into practice in our lives. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As they went on the way, a certain man said to him, “I want to follow you wherever you go, Lord.”
Jesus said to him, “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head.”
He said to another, “Follow me!” But he said, “Lord, allow me first to go and bury my father.”
But Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead, but you go and announce God’s Kingdom.”
Another also said, “I want to follow you, Lord, but first allow me to say good-bye to those who are at my house.”
But Jesus said to him, “No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for God’s Kingdom.”
b: This passage records three conversations between people and Jesus, showing the cost and resolve of following him. The first man eagerly said he would follow Jesus, but Jesus reminded him that following him meant having nowhere to lay one's head, with all the hardship and sacrifice that implies. The second man wanted to go home first and bury his father, which sounds like a reasonable request, yet Jesus told him that the work of God's kingdom comes before every worldly duty. The third man also said he would follow, but wanted to say goodbye to his family first. Jesus answered with the picture of a farmer plowing: following the Lord takes a whole heart, and there is no looking back.

This passage teaches us that following Jesus is more than an expression of feeling; it is a commitment of resolve and action. To follow Jesus means setting aside worldly comfort and ties and giving ourselves wholly to God's will. What Jesus asks for is unwavering faith and complete devotion. Whatever difficulty or temptation comes, we must not turn back.

This passage asks whether we are truly ready to give everything for God's kingdom. Are we willing to lay down every obstacle and follow Jesus with all our heart? On the path of following him, he calls us to a resolve that does not look back, and to lay down everything for his kingdom.
q: What things or relationships have become obstacles on your way of following Jesus? How can you follow God's will with greater single-mindedness?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for calling us to follow Jesus. Give us strength and resolve to let go of worldly entanglements and follow you with all our hearts, never turning back, whatever difficulties we face. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come.
Then he said to them, “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore to the Lord of the harvest, that he may send out laborers into his harvest.
Go your ways. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves.
Carry no purse, nor wallet, nor sandals. Greet no one on the way.
Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house.’
If a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.
Remain in that same house, eating and drinking the things they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Don’t go from house to house.
Into whatever city you enter, and they receive you, eat the things that are set before you.
Heal the sick who are there, and tell them, ‘God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
But into whatever city you enter, and they don’t receive you, go out into its streets and say,
‘Even the dust from your city that clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that God’s Kingdom has come near to you.’
I tell you, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city.
b: This passage tells how Jesus sent out seventy disciples, two by two, into every town and place, to prepare the way for his coming. Jesus told them that the harvest is plentiful but the workers are few, so they should ask the Lord to send out workers. He warned them that they were like lambs going among wolves and needed to stay alert and depend on God. He told them not to carry too many possessions and not to be distracted on the road, but to stay focused on their mission.

Jesus went on to teach that when they entered a house or town, they should first speak peace over it. If someone there welcomed them, their blessing would rest on that place; if no one did, the blessing would return to them. Jesus stressed that their mission was to announce that God's kingdom had come near. In the course of preaching they would meet both welcome and rejection, but in either case they were to complete the mission faithfully.

This passage reminds us that as followers of Jesus we too are called to go out and gather the harvest of God's kingdom. We need to answer this call in our own lives and become workers for the kingdom, holding fast to proclaiming God's gospel whatever challenges and difficulties we meet. Our faith and faithfulness matter greatly in this, because everything we do is service to God's kingdom.
q: Do you sense God's call in your life to take part in his work? How can you be a faithful worker for his kingdom in your own setting?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for calling us to be workers in your kingdom. Give us courage and wisdom to faithfully complete the mission you have entrusted to us, and to keep proclaiming your gospel whatever challenges we meet. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon which were done in you, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.
But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the judgment than for you.
You, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades.
Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me. Whoever rejects me rejects him who sent me.”
b: In this passage Jesus rebukes Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, cities that witnessed many mighty works in his ministry and still did not repent. Jesus says that if these miracles had been done in Tyre and Sidon, those Gentile cities would have repented long ago, and on the day of judgment they would receive a lighter punishment than these Jewish towns. Jesus then reminds the disciples that whoever listens to them listens to him, and whoever rejects them rejects him and the Father who sent him.

This passage stresses the importance of repentance. Miracles and wonders should move people to turn back to God, yet the people of Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum chose indifference and unbelief, and so will face serious consequences on the day of judgment. Jesus' words remind us that when we see God at work and hear his call, we must not be unmoved but respond with repentance and faith.

This passage also reminds us that as Jesus' disciples we carry the responsibility of passing on his message. Our words and conduct represent Jesus, and when people accept or reject our message, they are in fact accepting or rejecting him. So we should take our mission seriously and proclaim God's truth with faith and reverence.
q: How do you respond when you see God at work in your life? Is there anything you need to repent of, so that your relationship with God can be set right?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us, through Jesus Christ, how important repentance is. Help us to respond to what you do with humility and faith, so that we never ignore your call. May we faithfully proclaim your message, so that more people turn to you. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: The seventy returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!”
He said to them, “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven.
Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you.
Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”
b: In this passage the seventy disciples complete the mission Jesus gave them and return with joy to report what they experienced. They are amazed that even demons submit to them in Jesus' name, which shows the authority they have in the work of God's kingdom. Hearing their report, Jesus says that Satan's power is being broken, and he reminds them that they have been given authority to trample on evil, all because God's power is at work in them.

But Jesus goes on to teach that the true cause for joy is not their victory in spiritual warfare, but that their names are written in heaven. This reminds us that spiritual authority and power matter, yet our deepest joy should come from our identity in God's kingdom, an identity that is eternal and an expression of our relationship with God.

This passage reminds us that as Christians we should focus on our relationship with God rather than merely chasing spiritual power or achievements. God has given us authority to face spiritual challenges, but our real joy should come from knowing that we belong to him and have a share in his kingdom. Our eyes should be fixed on that eternal reward, not just on victories in this present life.
q: In your spiritual life, do you pay more attention to spiritual achievements than to your relationship with God? How can you more deeply experience the eternal joy of belonging to God's kingdom?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for giving us spiritual authority so that we can overcome in spiritual warfare. Yet help us always to remember that true joy comes from our eternal relationship with you. May our hearts stay fixed on the reward in heaven rather than on the achievements of this life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, and said, “I thank you, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight.”

Turning to the disciples, he said, “All things have been delivered to me by my Father. No one knows who the Son is, except the Father, and who the Father is, except the Son, and he to whomever the Son desires to reveal him.”
Turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes which see the things that you see,
for I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see the things which you see, and didn’t see them, and to hear the things which you hear, and didn’t hear them.”
b: This passage records Jesus rejoicing in the Holy Spirit and thanking the Father, because God has revealed the truths of his kingdom to little children and hidden them from the wise and understanding. Jesus stresses that knowing the deep truth of the Father and the Son does not come through human wisdom but through God's revelation. He then tells his disciples that they are blessed, because they see and hear what many prophets and kings longed to see and hear but could not.

This passage shows us the contrast between God's kingdom and worldly wisdom. God chooses to reveal his mysteries to those who trust him with a child's simplicity, not to those who rely on their own wisdom. It reminds us that spiritual insight and understanding come from God's revelation, not from human intellect or effort. Jesus also shows us that being able to witness the mysteries of God's kingdom is a great blessing.

This passage challenges us to keep a simple faith, not to lean on our own cleverness, and to be thankful for the truth God has shown us in our lives. It is by God's grace that we can know and experience his kingdom, so we should treasure what we have received.
q: In your pursuit of spiritual truth, do you rely more on your own wisdom? How can you depend more on God's revelation to know his kingdom more deeply?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for revealing the truth of your kingdom to us who trust you like little children. Help us always to keep that simplicity, not relying on our own cleverness but on your revelation to know you. May our hearts overflow with thanksgiving for the truth you have shown us. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: Behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
He said to him, “What is written in the law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.”
He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
b: In this passage a lawyer tests Jesus, asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus does not answer directly but leads the lawyer to reflect on what the law teaches. The lawyer quotes the two greatest commandments in the law: love God and love your neighbor. Jesus affirms the answer, stresses the importance of putting it into practice, and says that keeping these two commandments is the way to eternal life.

This passage stresses the importance of love: loving God means giving ourselves to him with all our heart, soul, strength and mind, while loving our neighbor means expressing selfless love and care for others. It tells us that true faith is more than knowledge in theory; it is lived out in daily life. Loving God and loving people are not separate things; they belong together and are the heart of faith.

In this passage Jesus reminds us that loving God and loving others are the most important commandments in our lives and the way to eternal life. Our faith should not stop at words or thoughts but should show itself in action. We need to keep asking ourselves whether we are truly practicing these two commandments, and whether we love our neighbors in daily life with a heart that loves God.
q: How can you better put the commandments to love God and love others into action in your life? What concrete ways could help you express your love for God and for others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us how important it is to love God and love people. Help us to practice these two commandments in daily life, to prove our love for you by our actions, and to care selflessly for our neighbors. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: But he, desiring to justify himself, asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?”
Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place, and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”
b: This passage is the well-known parable of the Good Samaritan. Through this story Jesus answers the lawyer's question, "Who is my neighbor?" The Samaritan, though his people had a deep history of hostility with the Jews, became a neighbor to the wounded man, because he helped this stranger with compassion and without holding anything back. The priest and the Levite, by contrast, as religious leaders, chose to ignore the man in need.

This passage challenges our narrow definition of "neighbor." Jesus teaches that true love for a neighbor goes beyond the boundaries of ethnicity, religion and social standing. Loving our neighbor is not only showing kindness to those we know and feel close to, but reaching out in our daily lives to everyone who needs help. This love is unconditional, a deep care for the whole human family.

Through this passage God tells us that true love is action, not just words or thoughts. Jesus asks us to "go and do likewise," to be the Samaritan who shows compassion and care to others. Wherever we are and whoever we meet, we are called to be a neighbor to them and to touch their lives with love and mercy.
q: Today, have you met someone who needs your help? How can you be more intentional about being a neighbor to others and showing the unconditional love Jesus taught?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for reminding us through Jesus' teaching that true love is unconditional and cares for everyone. Help us to be the Good Samaritan in our lives and to love our neighbors with our actions. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet, and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”
b: This passage tells the story of Martha and Mary. When Jesus came to their home, Martha was busy with preparations and serving, while Mary chose to sit at Jesus' feet and listen closely to his teaching. Martha was distracted and troubled by her busyness and complained that Mary was not helping her, but Jesus said that Mary had chosen "the good part," which would not be taken away from her.

This passage teaches us that in a busy life we should put spiritual pursuit first. Martha was doing good things, but she was driven by busyness and anxiety, and so lost the rest of being with the Lord. Mary seized the opportunity and gave herself to listening to Jesus, and her spiritual life was nourished and lifted. Jesus reminds us that spiritual pursuit and closeness to him should hold first place in our lives.

Through this passage God reminds us that in life we are often pulled in many directions, even by good things, but we should remember to stop regularly, focus on God, and seek intimacy with him. This is the foundation of our spiritual growth and the way to find true peace in a busy life.
q: In the busyness of life, do you often forget to pursue your spiritual life? Today, how can you rearrange your priorities to focus more on your relationship with God?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us how, in the middle of busyness, to focus on your word and your presence. Help us to seek the good part in life, so that our hearts can always rest in you. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.”
He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Give us day by day our daily bread.
Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ ”
b: In this passage Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray, giving us the prayer we know as the Lord's Prayer. It covers every part of a believer's life, from worshiping God and asking for his kingdom to come, to daily provision, forgiveness of sin, and protection from temptation. It is a complete pattern for prayer, teaching us how to bring every area of our lives into our praying.

The Lord's Prayer is more than a set of words; it is a guide for the spiritual life. First, Jesus stresses reverence for God and longing for his kingdom to come, reminding us that prayer should begin by focusing on God's will and his glory. Then Jesus teaches us to ask for our daily needs, acknowledging our dependence on God, and to ask for his forgiveness and protection, which stresses our spiritual dependence in daily life.

This passage reminds us that prayer is an indispensable part of a believer's life, and through prayer we keep an intimate relationship with God. The Lord's Prayer teaches us how to balance worship, thanksgiving, petition and repentance in prayer, and reminds us that in every area of life we should depend on God's guidance and provision.
q: Today, did your prayer include worship, thanksgiving, petition and repentance? How can you connect with God more deeply in prayer?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us how to pray through the Lord's Prayer. Help us to focus on your will in prayer and to depend on your grace and provision in every area of life. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight, and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread,
for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’
and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’?
I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs.
b: In this passage Jesus teaches his disciples about persistence in prayer. Through the parable of a friend who asks for help at midnight, Jesus stresses the importance of asking without giving up. The friend, disturbed in the middle of the night, may at first be unwilling to help, but because the one asking keeps on, he finally gets up and gives him what he needs.

This parable reminds us not to give up easily in prayer. Even when our requests seem to get no immediate answer, we should keep asking God, like the man in the parable. This shows our trust in God and also the urgency of what we ask. God delights when we come to him with firm faith, and he will answer us in his time.

Through this passage God encourages us to have patience and persistence in prayer. Prayer is not an occasional act but a way of staying continually connected with God. Our faith and patience are trained and strengthened in the process. God knows our needs, and as we keep praying, he prepares his grace and provision for us.
q: Have you ever felt discouraged in prayer? Today, how can you keep asking God with greater patience and faith?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching us to persevere in prayer. Give us faith and patience, so that we keep depending on you as we ask, and trust your promises and your timing. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
“Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he?
Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he?
If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”
b: In this passage Jesus again stresses the importance of prayer, and uses a simple illustration to explain God's love and generosity toward his people. Jesus encourages his disciples to keep asking, seeking and knocking, because the Father will surely answer their requests. He goes on to say that if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the best, the Holy Spirit, to those who ask him?

This passage reminds us that prayer is an act full of faith. Our Father is good and glad to bless, and he is willing to give us the power and guidance of the Holy Spirit in our lives. We should believe that God not only hears our prayers but wants to meet our needs, and to give us grace beyond all we ask or think.

Through this passage God teaches us to keep on asking and to trust his goodness. Our prayers are not in vain; God's promises are true. When we come to him in faith, he will answer us and give us the best, especially the presence and power of the Holy Spirit.
q: In your prayer life, do you trust God's promises and keep asking and seeking his guidance? Today, how can you trust God's goodness more and be more steadfast in prayer?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for being a Father full of love and generosity, who is willing to hear our prayers. Give us faith, so that we firmly believe you will fulfill your promises in our lives and send the Holy Spirit to guide us. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: He was casting out a demon, and it was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke; and the multitudes marveled.
But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of the demons.”
Others, testing him, sought from him a sign from heaven.
But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation. A house divided against itself falls.
If Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul.
But if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
But if I by God’s finger cast out demons, then God’s Kingdom has come to you.
b: This passage tells of the challenge and doubt Jesus faced after he drove out a demon that had made a man mute. Even though what Jesus did was an obvious miracle, some people questioned his power and even accused him of driving out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Jesus answered these accusations with wisdom, pointing out that Satan cannot fight against himself, for then his kingdom could not stand.

Jesus stresses that his power to drive out demons comes from God, which proves that God's kingdom has come among people. This passage reminds us that God's kingdom comes with his authority and power, and that what God does often challenges our beliefs. When we face miracles and wonders, we need to respond with faith rather than doubt, because God's power goes beyond our understanding.

Through this passage God tells us that his kingdom has been revealed in Jesus Christ, and we should be full of confidence in his authority and power. Even when we face challenges or doubts, we should still firmly believe that God's kingdom is at work in our lives and is changing them by his power.
q: When you face doubts or challenges about your faith, how do you keep trusting that God's kingdom and authority are at work in your life?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank you for revealing your kingdom and authority in Jesus Christ. Strengthen our faith, so that when we face challenges and doubts we still believe firmly in your power. May your kingdom keep expanding in our lives and show your glory. We pray in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
dc: Thank you, Holy Spirit, for leading us to understand the truth and to live it out. May God bless you.

v: “When the strong man, fully armed, guards his own dwelling, his goods are safe.
But when someone stronger attacks him and overcomes him, he takes from him his whole armor in which he trusted, and divides his plunder.
“He that is not with me is against me. He who doesn’t gather with me scatters.
The unclean spirit, when he has gone out of the man, passes through dry places, seeking rest, and finding none, he says, ‘I will turn back to my house from which I came out.’
When he returns, he finds it swept and put in order.
Then he goes, and takes seven other spirits more evil than himself, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first.”
b: In this passage Jesus uses a parable to warn his disciples and remind them of the reality of spiritual warfare. He says that when a strong man guards his own house, all is at peace, but if someone stronger comes and takes his goods, he loses everything. This parable reveals a truth about spiritual warfare: in the spiritual realm we need to depend on a power stronger than ours, God's power, to protect us from the attacks of evil.
